chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskhan, from Mansur al-Sayqal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a broken sword that is sold for dirhams, and he said: 'If its silver content is less than the coinage value, there is no objection; but if its silver content is more, it is not suitable.'

key_terms.فَلاَ بَأْسَ: There is no objection / it is permissible
key_terms.فَلاَ يَصْلُحُ: It is not suitable / not permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a broken sword based on its silver content versus its face value in dirhams?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the permissibility of selling a broken sword by distinguishing between its value as a commodity and its value as currency; if its silver content is less than the dirham value, the sale is valid, but if it exceeds it, the sale is invalid due to the risk of riba (usury) in unequal exchange. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of evaluating mixed-value items based on their intrinsic metallic worth relative to standard currency to ensure fairness in trade. The distinction underscores the importance of preventing hidden usury in transactions involving precious metals, a key concern in Islamic commercial law.
